title: Concept Drills — Classification of Elements & Periodic Table (Class 11 Chemistry)
subject: chemistry

questions.concept: Atomic radius trend and its cause
questions.question: Why does atomic radius DECREASE across a period but INCREASE down a group?
questions.solution: Across a period, protons are added to the same shell — nuclear charge rises while shielding barely changes, pulling electrons in (radius shrinks). Down a group, a new shell is added each period — the outer electrons sit farther out and are shielded by inner shells (radius grows). Effective nuclear charge vs shell number is the tug-of-war.

questions.question: Why is boron's first ionisation energy LOWER than beryllium's, breaking the across-period trend?
questions.solution: Be: 2s² — a paired, penetrating s electron. B: 2s²2p¹ — the new electron sits in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and less penetrating than 2s, so it is easier to remove. Subshell energy (2p above 2s) overrides the general nuclear-charge trend. Similar dips occur at O (paired p electron repulsion) vs N.

questions.question: Distinguish electron affinity from electronegativity, and explain why both peak near fluorine.
questions.solution: Electron affinity: the energy change when an ISOLATED gaseous atom gains an electron (a measurable process). Electronegativity: the TENDENCY of a BONDED atom to attract shared electrons (a derived, relative number). Both peak near F because a small atom with high nuclear charge and nearly full shell holds added/shared electrons most strongly — small size + high effective charge.

questions.question: Why is metallic character highest at the bottom-left of the periodic table and lowest at the top-right?
questions.solution: Metallic character = ease of LOSING electrons. Bottom-left: large atoms, low ionisation energy, outer electrons loosely held — easily lost. Top-right: small atoms, high ionisation energy plus high electron affinity — electrons gained, not lost. The diagonal from Cs/Fr to F marks the metal-to-nonmetal gradient.

questions.question: Why do lithium resemble magnesium and beryllium resemble aluminium in chemistry?
questions.solution: Diagonal neighbours have similar charge/size ratios: Li⁺ and Mg²⁺ are similar in size and polarising power, as are Be²⁺ and Al³⁺. Similar polarising power → similar covalent character of compounds and similar solubility/thermal behaviour. The diagonal pairs' properties converge because size decrease and charge increase across the period offset each other.
